claim: Two-dimensional (2D) human skeletal muscle fiber cultures are ill-equipped to support the contractile properties of maturing muscle fibers.
source: Two-dimensional (2D) human skeletal muscle fiber cultures are ill-equipped to support the contractile properties of maturing muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a motivation for the study.

claim: The contractile limitation of 2D cultures limits their application to the study of adult human neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development.
source: This limits their application to the study of adult human neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development, a process requiring maturation of muscle fibers in the presence of motor neuron endplates.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the 2D culture limitation in the abstract.

claim: Adult human NMJ development requires maturation of muscle fibers in the presence of motor neuron endplates.
source: This limits their application to the study of adult human neuromuscular junction (NMJ) development, a process requiring maturation of muscle fibers in the presence of motor neuron endplates.
evidence: This is stated as a known requirement for NMJ development.

claim: A three-dimensional (3D) co-culture method enables human muscle progenitors mixed with human pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons to self-organize to form functional NMJ connections.
source: Here we describe a three-dimensional (3D) co-culture method whereby human muscle progenitors mixed with human pluripotent stem cell-derived motor neurons self-organize to form functional NMJ connections.
evidence: This is the main finding described in the abstract.

claim: Functional connectivity between motor neuron endplates and muscle fibers is confirmed with calcium imaging.
source: Functional connectivity between motor neuron endplates and muscle fibers is confirmed with calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to confirm functional connectivity.

claim: Functional connectivity between motor neuron endplates and muscle fibers is confirmed with electrophysiological recordings.
source: Functional connectivity between motor neuron endplates and muscle fibers is confirmed with calcium imaging and electrophysiological recordings.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to confirm functional connectivity.

claim: Epsilon acetylcholine receptor subunit protein upregulation is only observed in 3D co-cultures.
source: Notably, we only observed epsilon acetylcholine receptor subunit protein upregulation and activity in 3D co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: Epsilon acetylcholine receptor subunit activity is only observed in 3D co-cultures.
source: Notably, we only observed epsilon acetylcholine receptor subunit protein upregulation and activity in 3D co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the abstract.

claim: 3D co-culture treatments with myasthenia gravis patient sera demonstrates the ease of studying human disease with the system.
source: Further, 3D co-culture treatments with myasthenia gravis patient sera shows the ease of studying human disease with the system.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstration of the system's utility.

claim: The skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a highly organized synapse formed between a motor neuron (MN) axon and a muscle fiber.
source: The skeletal muscle neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a highly organized synapse formed between a motor neuron (MN) axon and a muscle fiber.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The NMJ is designed to transmit efferent signals from projecting MNs to muscle fibers in order to actuate fiber contraction.
source: It is designed to transmit efferent signals from projecting MNs to muscle fibers in order to actuate fiber contraction.
evidence: This is stated as the function of the NMJ.

claim: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) clustered at the NMJ's postsynaptic muscle fiber membrane mediate signal transmission by binding acetylcholine (ACh) neurotransmitters released from vesicles at the presynaptic MN axon terminal.
source: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChRs) clustered at the NMJ's postsynaptic muscle fiber membrane mediate this signal by binding acetylcholine (ACh) neurotransmitters released from vesicles at the presynaptic MN axon terminal.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of signal transmission at the NMJ.

claim: AChRs are ligand-gated ion channels composed of five protein subunits.
source: AChRs are ligand-gated ion channels composed of five protein subunits.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of AChRs.

claim: During development the gamma subunit in embryonic AChRs is replaced by an epsilon subunit in the adult synapse.
source: During development the gamma subunit in embryonic AChRs is replaced by an epsilon subunit in the adult synapse (Mishina et al., 1986; Missias et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as a known developmental process with citations.

claim: Previous animal studies showed that the AChR subunit transition occurs in the presence of motor axon endplates.
source: Previous animal studies showed that this AChR subunit transition occurs in the presence of motor axon endplates and confirmed that transcription of the epsilon gene (CHRNE) is stimulated by AChR Inducing Activity (ARIA) via ErbB receptors, a nerve derived ligand of the neuregulin-1 (NRG1) family (Martinou et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous animal studies with citation.

claim: Transcription of the epsilon gene (CHRNE) is stimulated by AChR Inducing Activity (ARIA) via ErbB receptors, a nerve derived ligand of the neuregulin-1 (NRG1) family.
source: Previous animal studies showed that this AChR subunit transition occurs in the presence of motor axon endplates and confirmed that transcription of the epsilon gene (CHRNE) is stimulated by AChR Inducing Activity (ARIA) via ErbB receptors, a nerve derived ligand of the neuregulin-1 (NRG1) family (Martinou et al., 1991).
evidence: This is stated as a confirmed mechanism with citation.

claim: CHRNE transcripts are detected in rodent 2D and 3D skeletal muscle fiber cultures when co-cultured with nerve cells.
source: Consistently, CHRNE transcripts are detected in rodent 2D and 3D skeletal muscle fiber cultures when co-cultured with nerve cells (Bach et al., 2003; Ostrovidov et al., 2017; Smith et al., 2016; Vilmont et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a consistent finding with citations.

claim: The first reports of human NMJ models do not demonstrate synapse maturation via the gamma to epsilon AChR subunit switch.
source: However, despite significant progress toward directing human pluripotent stem cells (PSCs) to the motor neuron lineage (Ashton et al., 2015; Hu and Zhang, 2010; Lippmann et al., 2014; Maury et al., 2015; Shimojo et al., 2015; Zhang et al., 2001) and establishing electrically and chemically responsive human muscle fibers in vitro (Madden et al., 2015), the first reports of human NMJ models – 2D (Guo et al., 2011; Santhanam et al., 2018; Steinbeck et al., 2016) or 3D (Maffioletti et al., 2018; Osaki et al., 2018) human muscle fiber and motor neuron co-cultures – do not demonstrate synapse maturation via the gamma to epsilon AChR subunit switch.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of existing models with citations.

claim: There are no reports of epsilon AChR protein expression or function in culture in the absence of enforced gene expression.
source: Further, there are no reports of epsilon AChR protein expression or function in culture in the absence of enforced gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature.

claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome is one of the most prevalent genetic diseases of the NMJ.
source: Congenital myasthenic syndrome is one of the most prevalent genetic diseases of the NMJ and commonly arises from mutations in one of the AChR encoding genes (Engel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Congenital myasthenic syndrome commonly arises from mutations in one of the AChR encoding genes.
source: Congenital myasthenic syndrome is one of the most prevalent genetic diseases of the NMJ and commonly arises from mutations in one of the AChR encoding genes (Engel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: The vast majority of mutations causing congenital myasthenic syndrome arise in the CHRNE gene, the adult specific subunit of the AChR.
source: The vast majority of mutations causing the disease arise in the CHRNE gene, the adult specific subunit of the AChR (Abicht et al., 2012; Engel et al., 1993).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citations.

claim: There is a lack of effective therapies for a wide range of neuromuscular diseases impacting the adult NMJ.
source: Given the lack of effective therapies for a wide range of neuromuscular diseases impacting the adult NMJ (Ohno et al., 1999), and that the majority of AChR mutations are mutations of the CHRNE gene (Ohno et al., 1995), a robust method to model the adult human NMJ in a dish is needed to synergize with recent advances in differentiating patient-derived PSCs to the MN lineage (Chen et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2010; Lorenz et al., 2017; Sances et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a motivation for the study with citation.

claim: The majority of AChR mutations are mutations of the CHRNE gene.
source: Given the lack of effective therapies for a wide range of neuromuscular diseases impacting the adult NMJ (Ohno et al., 1999), and that the majority of AChR mutations are mutations of the CHRNE gene (Ohno et al., 1995), a robust method to model the adult human NMJ in a dish is needed to synergize with recent advances in differentiating patient-derived PSCs to the MN lineage (Chen et al., 2011; Hu et al., 2010; Lorenz et al., 2017; Sances et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: The method enables de novo formation of the adult human NMJ in as early as two weeks.
source: Here we report a method integrating architectural cues with co-culture techniques to create an environment conducive to the de novo formation of the adult human NMJ in as early as two weeks.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding of the study.

claim: The 3D culture system enables long-term maintenance of maturing muscle fibers in culture.
source: In side-by-side studies of muscle fibers cultured in 2D, we show that the 3D culture system enables long-term maintenance of maturing muscle fibers in culture.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparative studies.

claim: The 3D culture system supports the formation and morphological maturation of AChR clusters primed for synaptogenesis.
source: It supports the formation and morphological maturation of AChR clusters primed for synaptogenesis and the de novo transition from the embryonic to the adult NMJ composition upon contact with MN endplates.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: The 3D culture system supports the de novo transition from the embryonic to the adult NMJ composition upon contact with MN endplates.
source: It supports the formation and morphological maturation of AChR clusters primed for synaptogenesis and the de novo transition from the embryonic to the adult NMJ composition upon contact with MN endplates.
evidence: This is stated as a finding of the study.

claim: Formation of functional NMJ connections is confirmed by imaging muscle fiber calcium transients in response to glutamate-induced MN firing.
source: We confirm formation of functional NMJ connections by imaging muscle fiber calcium transients and capturing electrophysiological recordings in response to glutamate-induced MN firing and demonstrate that treatment with inhibitors targeting pre- and post-synapse function block this firing.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to confirm functional connections.

claim: Formation of functional NMJ connections is confirmed by capturing electrophysiological recordings in response to glutamate-induced MN firing.
source: We confirm formation of functional NMJ connections by imaging muscle fiber calcium transients and capturing electrophysiological recordings in response to glutamate-induced MN firing and demonstrate that treatment with inhibitors targeting pre- and post-synapse function block this firing.
evidence: This is stated as a method used to confirm functional connections.

claim: Treatment with inhibitors targeting pre- and post-synapse function block glutamate-induced MN firing.
source: We confirm formation of functional NMJ connections by imaging muscle fiber calcium transients and capturing electrophysiological recordings in response to glutamate-induced MN firing and demonstrate that treatment with inhibitors targeting pre- and post-synapse function block this firing.
evidence: This is stated as a finding demonstrating functional connectivity.

claim: The 3D co-culture platform, and not a 2D co-culture system, supports the transition from the embryonic to the adult AChR.
source: We show that the 3D co-culture platform, and not a 2D co-culture system, supports the transition from the embryonic to the adult AChR, thereby enabling the functional assessment of the adult neuromuscular junction in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding comparing 2D and 3D systems.

claim: The 3D co-culture platform enables the functional assessment of the adult neuromuscular junction in vitro.
source: We show that the 3D co-culture platform, and not a 2D co-culture system, supports the transition from the embryonic to the adult AChR, thereby enabling the functional assessment of the adult neuromuscular junction in vitro.
evidence: This is stated as a capability enabled by the 3D system.

claim: Data aligns with prior studies showing that epsilon functional activity is regulated post-transcriptionally.
source: We present data aligning with prior studies showing that epsilon functional activity is regulated post-transcriptionally (Bruneau et al., 2005; Caroni et al., 1993; Jayawickreme and Claudio, 1994; Khan et al., 2014; Missias et al., 1996; Ross et al., 1991; Wild et al., 2016; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and in particular, supports work indicating a role for innervation (spontaneous miniature endplate potentials) and/or muscle fiber maturation in encouraging subunit substitution (Caroni et al., 1993; Missias et al., 1996; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding that aligns with prior work with citations.

claim: Data supports work indicating a role for innervation (spontaneous miniature endplate potentials) in encouraging subunit substitution.
source: We present data aligning with prior studies showing that epsilon functional activity is regulated post-transcriptionally (Bruneau et al., 2005; Caroni et al., 1993; Jayawickreme and Claudio, 1994; Khan et al., 2014; Missias et al., 1996; Ross et al., 1991; Wild et al., 2016; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and in particular, supports work indicating a role for innervation (spontaneous miniature endplate potentials) and/or muscle fiber maturation in encouraging subunit substitution (Caroni et al., 1993; Missias et al., 1996; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding that supports prior work with citations.

claim: Data supports work indicating a role for muscle fiber maturation in encouraging subunit substitution.
source: We present data aligning with prior studies showing that epsilon functional activity is regulated post-transcriptionally (Bruneau et al., 2005; Caroni et al., 1993; Jayawickreme and Claudio, 1994; Khan et al., 2014; Missias et al., 1996; Ross et al., 1991; Wild et al., 2016; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and in particular, supports work indicating a role for innervation (spontaneous miniature endplate potentials) and/or muscle fiber maturation in encouraging subunit substitution (Caroni et al., 1993; Missias et al., 1996; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as a finding that supports prior work with citations.

claim: Treatment of neuromuscular co-cultures with IgG purified from myasthenia gravis (MG) patient sera together with human complement results in readily visible clinical-like phenotypes in as early as two weeks of culture time.
source: Finally, we demonstrate the versatility and ease of the system for modeling human disease by treating neuromuscular co-cultures with IgG purified from myasthenia gravis (MG) patient sera together with human complement, which results in readily visible clinical-like phenotypes in as early as two weeks of culture time.
evidence: This is stated as a demonstration of the system's utility for disease modeling.

claim: Muscle fibers in 3D tissues progressively increased in diameter over three weeks in culture.
source: In contrast to the muscle fibers established in 2D cultures, those derived in 3D culture progressively increased in diameter over three weeks in culture (Figure 1B) while maintaining fiber alignment and assembled contractile apparatus (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1B showing quantification of fiber diameter over time.

claim: 3D muscle tissues upregulated expression of the fast and slow adult isoforms of myosin heavy chain (MHC) over time.
source: Furthermore, over time in 3D culture, muscle tissues upregulated expression of the fast and slow adult isoforms of myosin heavy chain (MHC), which was accompanied by a downregulation of embryonic MHC expression, suggesting a gradual sarcomere structural maturation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C and supplementary figures showing western blot data.

claim: Upregulation of adult MHC isoforms in 3D culture was accompanied by a downregulation of embryonic MHC expression.
source: Furthermore, over time in 3D culture, muscle tissues upregulated expression of the fast and slow adult isoforms of myosin heavy chain (MHC), which was accompanied by a downregulation of embryonic MHC expression, suggesting a gradual sarcomere structural maturation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by Figure 1C showing western blot data.

claim: The changes in MHC expression suggest a gradual sarcomere structural maturation in 3D culture.
source: Furthermore, over time in 3D culture, muscle tissues upregulated expression of the fast and slow adult isoforms of myosin heavy chain (MHC), which was accompanied by a downregulation of embryonic MHC expression, suggesting a gradual sarcomere structural maturation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the MHC expression data.

claim: There was an increased incidence of damaged fibers observed in 2D cultures.
source: The absence of these trends in 2D muscle fiber culture may be explained by the inability of tissue culture plastic to support muscle fiber contraction resulting in the increased incidence of damaged fibers observed in 2D cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and an enrichment of small, immature fibers (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to supplementary figures.

claim: 2D cultures showed an enrichment of small, immature fibers.
source: The absence of these trends in 2D muscle fiber culture may be explained by the inability of tissue culture plastic to support muscle fiber contraction resulting in the increased incidence of damaged fibers observed in 2D cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) and an enrichment of small, immature fibers (Figure 1A–B and Figure 1—figure supplement 2G–H).
evidence: This is stated as an observation with reference to figures.

claim: 3D human muscle tissues were capable of generating active force in as early as 10 days of differentiation as evidenced by spontaneous twitches.
source: In support of our molecular characterization, 3D human muscle tissues were capable of generating active force in as early as 10 days of differentiation as evidenced by spontaneous twitches (Video 1), which were not observed in 2D cultures.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 1.

claim: Spontaneous twitches were not observed in 2D cultures.
source: In support of our molecular characterization, 3D human muscle tissues were capable of generating active force in as early as 10 days of differentiation as evidenced by spontaneous twitches (Video 1), which were not observed in 2D cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between 2D and 3D cultures.

claim: Two-week old 3D muscle tissue twitch response could be paced by low frequency electrical stimuli (1 Hz).
source: Consistent with prior reports (Madden et al., 2015), two-week old 3D muscle tissue twitch response could be paced by low frequency electrical stimuli (1 Hz; Video 1), which converted into tetanus contractions in response to increased frequency (20 Hz; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation consistent with prior reports and supported by Video 1.

claim: Low frequency electrical stimuli (1 Hz) converted into tetanus contractions in response to increased frequency (20 Hz) in 3D muscle tissues.
source: Consistent with prior reports (Madden et al., 2015), two-week old 3D muscle tissue twitch response could be paced by low frequency electrical stimuli (1 Hz; Video 1), which converted into tetanus contractions in response to increased frequency (20 Hz; Video 1).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 1.

claim: ACh stimulation (10 μM) produced an immediate tetanus response in 3D tissues.
source: Similarly, ACh stimulation (10 μM) produced an immediate tetanus response (Video 1) in 3D tissues suggesting an abundance of active AChRs, while the response of 2D muscle fiber cultures at this time-point was significantly less and inevitably resulted in muscle fiber damage and/or release from the culture substrate (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 1.

claim: ACh stimulation suggests an abundance of active AChRs in 3D tissues.
source: Similarly, ACh stimulation (10 μM) produced an immediate tetanus response (Video 1) in 3D tissues suggesting an abundance of active AChRs, while the response of 2D muscle fiber cultures at this time-point was significantly less and inevitably resulted in muscle fiber damage and/or release from the culture substrate (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the ACh stimulation response.

claim: The response of 2D muscle fiber cultures to ACh stimulation was significantly less than 3D cultures and inevitably resulted in muscle fiber damage and/or release from the culture substrate.
source: Similarly, ACh stimulation (10 μM) produced an immediate tetanus response (Video 1) in 3D tissues suggesting an abundance of active AChRs, while the response of 2D muscle fiber cultures at this time-point was significantly less and inevitably resulted in muscle fiber damage and/or release from the culture substrate (Video 2).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison between 2D and 3D cultures supported by Video 2.

claim: Muscle fibers in 3D tissues generated strong collective calcium transient in response to electrical stimulation.
source: Muscle fibers in 3D tissues generated strong collective calcium transient in response to electrical stimulation and immediately following exposure to ACh (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures and video.

claim: Muscle fibers in 3D tissues generated strong collective calcium transient immediately following exposure to ACh.
source: Muscle fibers in 3D tissues generated strong collective calcium transient in response to electrical stimulation and immediately following exposure to ACh (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C and Video 3).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures and video.

claim: 3D muscle tissues generated using optogenetically-responsive muscle progenitor cells contracted in response to light stimulation on the second week of the culture.
source: 3D muscle tissues generated using optogenetically-responsive muscle progenitor cells contracted in response to light stimulation on the second week of the culture (Video 4).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 4.

claim: Light activation of ChR2 transduced muscle fibers generated a clear depolarization of the membrane potential.
source: As expected, recordings of 3D muscle prior to light stimulation revealed little electrical activity (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E), while light activation generated a clear depolarization of the membrane potential (Figure 1—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Passing depolarizing current led to regenerative potentials that become faster with increasing depolarization in 3D muscle fibers.
source: Passing depolarizing current led to regenerative potentials that become faster with increasing depolarization (Figure 1—figure supplement 3G).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: There was significantly higher expression of the nAChR-β protein in 3D compared to 2D cultures at 2 weeks of fiber differentiation.
source: We observed significantly higher expression of the nAChR-β protein in 3D compared to 2D cultures at 2 weeks of fiber differentiation (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and 2F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by figures showing western blot data.

claim: There was a greater number of AChR clusters per muscle fiber established in 3D compared to 2D culture.
source: Further, our analyses revealed a greater number of AChR clusters per muscle fiber established in 3D compared to 2D culture (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1E.

claim: At 2 weeks of culture, the majority of muscle fibers in 2D cultures lacked AChR clusters.
source: Indeed, we noted that at 2 weeks of culture, the majority of muscle fibers in 2D cultures lacked AChR clusters (Figure 1A and E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1A and E.

claim: There was a high frequency of branched and perforated AChR clusters in 3D muscle cultures.
source: Interestingly, although average AChR cluster area was not significantly different (Figure 1F), we observed a high frequency of branched and perforated AChR clusters in our 3D muscle cultures, whereas oval shaped AChR clusters dominated on muscle fibers cultured in 2D conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1D.

claim: Oval shaped AChR clusters dominated on muscle fibers cultured in 2D conditions.
source: Interestingly, although average AChR cluster area was not significantly different (Figure 1F), we observed a high frequency of branched and perforated AChR clusters in our 3D muscle cultures, whereas oval shaped AChR clusters dominated on muscle fibers cultured in 2D conditions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 1D.

claim: AChR clusters formed in 3D cultures had significantly higher average lacunarity compared to 2D cultures.
source: Lacunarity calculated from box counting validated our qualitative observations by indicating a significantly higher average lacunarity of AChR clusters formed in 3D cultures compared to 2D cultures (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding supported by Figure 1G.

claim: The 3D culture method better supports rapid contractile apparatus maturation and function compared to 2D culture.
source: Overall our comparison of muscle fibers established in 2D and 3D formats suggests that the 3D culture method better supports rapid contractile apparatus maturation and function, as well as AChR clustering and morphological maturation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: The 3D culture method better supports AChR clustering and morphological maturation compared to 2D culture.
source: Overall our comparison of muscle fibers established in 2D and 3D formats suggests that the 3D culture method better supports rapid contractile apparatus maturation and function, as well as AChR clustering and morphological maturation.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the comparative analysis.

claim: Muscle fiber maturation is a prerequisite for NMJ development.
source: Since muscle fiber maturation is a prerequisite for NMJ development (Fox, 2009), we evaluated the hypothesis that the 3D skeletal muscle tissue platform would be well suited for human PSC-derived MN incorporation to model human NMJ synaptogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: MN clusters were enriched (>85%) for cells expressing the HB9 and ISL1 transcription factors as well as the mature neurofilament marker SMI32.
source: Resulting MN clusters were enriched (>85%) for cells expressing the HB9 and ISL1 transcription factors as well as the mature neurofilament marker SMI32 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is stated as a characterization of the MN clusters supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Co-cultures self-organized such that muscle progenitor cells fused to form multinucleated, aligned and striated muscle fibers.
source: Immunostaining co-cultures on the second week of culture for the motor neuron marker SMI-32, muscle fiber marker sarcomeric α-actinin, and α-bungarotoxin (to visualize AChRs) revealed that the co-cultures self-organized such that muscle progenitor cells fused to form multinucleated, aligned and striated muscle fibers and the MN clusters were positioned at the periphery of muscle bundles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2B.

claim: MN clusters were positioned at the periphery of muscle bundles in co-cultures.
source: Immunostaining co-cultures on the second week of culture for the motor neuron marker SMI-32, muscle fiber marker sarcomeric α-actinin, and α-bungarotoxin (to visualize AChRs) revealed that the co-cultures self-organized such that muscle progenitor cells fused to form multinucleated, aligned and striated muscle fibers and the MN clusters were positioned at the periphery of muscle bundles (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2B.

claim: MNs were capable of regrowing neurites that were found in contact with α-bungarotoxin positive AChR clusters on muscle fibers.
source: Importantly, the MNs were capable of regrowing neurites that were found in contact with α-bungarotoxin positive AChR clusters on muscle fibers (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2B-C.

claim: Postsynaptic AChR aggregation on muscle fibers is supported by agrin secretion from MN axon terminals.
source: In vivo studies by others found that postsynaptic AChR aggregation on muscle fibers is supported by agrin secretion from MN axon terminals (Gautam et al., 1996).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge from in vivo studies with citation.

claim: Agrin is expressed in PSC-derived MN cultures.
source: We confirmed agrin expression in our PSC-derived MN cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated as a confirmation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Western blot analysis of neuromuscular co-cultures confirmed expression of MuSK protein.
source: Furthermore, western blot analysis of neuromuscular co-cultures confirmed expression of MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and rapsyn (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) proteins, two decisive synaptic proteins for mediating agrin-induced synaptogenesis (Glass and Yancopoulos, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Western blot analysis of neuromuscular co-cultures confirmed expression of rapsyn protein.
source: Furthermore, western blot analysis of neuromuscular co-cultures confirmed expression of MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and rapsyn (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) proteins, two decisive synaptic proteins for mediating agrin-induced synaptogenesis (Glass and Yancopoulos, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures.

claim: MuSK and rapsyn are two decisive synaptic proteins for mediating agrin-induced synaptogenesis.
source: Furthermore, western blot analysis of neuromuscular co-cultures confirmed expression of MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and rapsyn (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B) proteins, two decisive synaptic proteins for mediating agrin-induced synaptogenesis (Glass and Yancopoulos, 1997).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: The prevalence of rapsyn co-localization with bungaroxin-labeled AChR clusters was substantially higher in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures compared to muscle-alone cultures.
source: By comparison, the prevalence of rapsyn (Figure 2D) and MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) co-localization with bungaroxin-labeled AChR clusters was substantially higher in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures, but was not observed on all fibers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: The prevalence of MuSK co-localization with bungaroxin-labeled AChR clusters was substantially higher in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures compared to muscle-alone cultures.
source: By comparison, the prevalence of rapsyn (Figure 2D) and MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) co-localization with bungaroxin-labeled AChR clusters was substantially higher in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures, but was not observed on all fibers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Rapsyn and MuSK co-localization with AChR clusters was not observed on all fibers in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: By comparison, the prevalence of rapsyn (Figure 2D) and MuSK (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) co-localization with bungaroxin-labeled AChR clusters was substantially higher in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures, but was not observed on all fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a qualification of the observation.

claim: More and larger α-bungarotoxin positive AChR clusters were observed in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures as compared to 3D muscle-alone cultures.
source: Consistently, we observed more and larger α-bungarotoxin positive AChR clusters in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures as compared to 3D muscle-alone cultures (Figure 2E–G), particularly at sites where MN neurites contacted muscle fibers (Figure 2B, yellow boxes).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2E-G.

claim: More and larger AChR clusters were particularly observed at sites where MN neurites contacted muscle fibers.
source: Consistently, we observed more and larger α-bungarotoxin positive AChR clusters in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures as compared to 3D muscle-alone cultures (Figure 2E–G), particularly at sites where MN neurites contacted muscle fibers (Figure 2B, yellow boxes).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2B.

claim: There was a higher frequency of perforated and branched AChR clusters in 3D co-cultures as evidenced by the higher lacunarity of AChR clusters formed in co-cultures.
source: In addition, we observed a higher frequency of perforated and branched AChR clusters in our 3D co-cultures as evidenced by the higher lacunarity of AChR clusters formed in co-cultures (Figure 2H) supporting a role for motor axon derived factors in post synaptic differentiation of the NMJ.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2H.

claim: The higher lacunarity of AChR clusters in co-cultures supports a role for motor axon derived factors in post synaptic differentiation of the NMJ.
source: In addition, we observed a higher frequency of perforated and branched AChR clusters in our 3D co-cultures as evidenced by the higher lacunarity of AChR clusters formed in co-cultures (Figure 2H) supporting a role for motor axon derived factors in post synaptic differentiation of the NMJ.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the lacunarity data.

claim: Supplementing 3D human muscle tissue media with neural agrin (50 ng/mL) phenocopied the co-culture results.
source: As expected, by supplementing 3D human muscle tissue media with neural agrin (50 ng/mL) we phenocopied these co-culture results (Figure 2I–K).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 2I-K.

claim: The LAMB2 gene encoding for the laminin beta two chain was expressed by 3D human muscle tissues and neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: In further support of 3D muscle fiber synaptogenic maturation, the LAMB2 gene encoding for the laminin beta two chain was expressed by 3D human muscle tissues and neuromuscular co-cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G), and the protein was found enriched at AChR clusters (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures and Figure 2L.

claim: Laminin beta two protein was found enriched at AChR clusters.
source: In further support of 3D muscle fiber synaptogenic maturation, the LAMB2 gene encoding for the laminin beta two chain was expressed by 3D human muscle tissues and neuromuscular co-cultures (Figure 2—figure supplement 2G), and the protein was found enriched at AChR clusters (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 2L.

claim: Laminin beta two is concentrated at the neuromuscular junction synaptic cleft.
source: This is consistent with prior reports demonstrating laminin beta two concentrated at the neuromuscular junction synaptic cleft (Hunter et al., 1989) and the involvement of this tissue restricted basement membrane protein in NMJ maturation and maintenance (Noakes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Laminin beta two is involved in NMJ maturation and maintenance.
source: This is consistent with prior reports demonstrating laminin beta two concentrated at the neuromuscular junction synaptic cleft (Hunter et al., 1989) and the involvement of this tissue restricted basement membrane protein in NMJ maturation and maintenance (Noakes et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge with citation.

claim: Human PSC-derived MNs exocytose in response to potassium chloride (KCl, 60 mM) stimuli.
source: Using the fluorescent styryl dye FM 1–43 (Gaffield and Betz, 2006) and confocal microscopy we performed exocytosis assays on differentiated MNs (Day 20) and confirmed that human PSC-derived MNs exocytose in response to potassium chloride (KCl, 60 mM) and the excitatory neurotransmitter, L-glutamate (50 μM) stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures and video.

claim: Human PSC-derived MNs exocytose in response to the excitatory neurotransmitter, L-glutamate (50 μM) stimuli.
source: Using the fluorescent styryl dye FM 1–43 (Gaffield and Betz, 2006) and confocal microscopy we performed exocytosis assays on differentiated MNs (Day 20) and confirmed that human PSC-derived MNs exocytose in response to potassium chloride (KCl, 60 mM) and the excitatory neurotransmitter, L-glutamate (50 μM) stimuli (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–D and Video 5).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures and video.

claim: The amino acid glutamate is a neurotransmitter that specifically stimulates MN cells but not muscle fibers.
source: The latter is particularly important, since the amino acid glutamate is a neurotransmitter that specifically stimulates MN cells but not muscle fibers (50 μM; Video 3).
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge supported by Video 3.

claim: Calcium transients and synchronous tissue contractions were observed in muscle fibers in close proximity to the MN clusters in as early as 14 days of co-culture following glutamate stimulation.
source: Next, we stimulated neuromuscular co-cultures that were generated using GCaMP6 transduced muscle progenitor cells with a 50 μM glutamate solution and observed calcium transients (Figure 3A–B and Video 6) and synchronous tissue contractions (Figure 3C and Video 7) in the muscle fibers in close proximity to the MN clusters in as early as 14 days of co-culture, indicating the formation of functional connectivity between MN endplates and muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by figures and videos.

claim: Glutamate-induced calcium transients and contractions indicate the formation of functional connectivity between MN endplates and muscle fibers.
source: Next, we stimulated neuromuscular co-cultures that were generated using GCaMP6 transduced muscle progenitor cells with a 50 μM glutamate solution and observed calcium transients (Figure 3A–B and Video 6) and synchronous tissue contractions (Figure 3C and Video 7) in the muscle fibers in close proximity to the MN clusters in as early as 14 days of co-culture, indicating the formation of functional connectivity between MN endplates and muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the glutamate stimulation results.

claim: Many, but not all the fibers were functionally innervated in neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: Our analysis of this serial stimulation data revealed that many, but not all the fibers were functionally innervated (Figure 3A–B and Video 6).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from serial stimulation experiments.

claim: Direct stimulation of AChRs using ACh led to higher co-culture contractile force generation compared to glutamate stimulation.
source: As expected, direct stimulation of AChRs using ACh led to higher co-culture contractile force generation as quantified by tissue movement (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Figure 3C.

claim: BOTOX treatment resulted in a significant decrease in calcium transient activity and an absence of tissue contraction in response to glutamate stimulation.
source: Our studies revealed a significant decrease in calcium transient activity and an absence of tissue contraction in response to glutamate stimulation if neuromuscular co-cultures were pre-treated with BOTOX or d-tubocurarine (Figure 3D and Video 7) doses reported by others to fully block activity (Ko et al., 2019; Madden et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 3D and video.

claim: d-tubocurarine treatment resulted in a significant decrease in calcium transient activity and an absence of tissue contraction in response to glutamate stimulation.
source: Our studies revealed a significant decrease in calcium transient activity and an absence of tissue contraction in response to glutamate stimulation if neuromuscular co-cultures were pre-treated with BOTOX or d-tubocurarine (Figure 3D and Video 7) doses reported by others to fully block activity (Ko et al., 2019; Madden et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 3D and video.

claim: Very few functional connections were observed when evaluating 2D neuromuscular co-cultures matured for 2 weeks and then treated with glutamate.
source: In contrast, and as expected, we observed very few functional connections when evaluating 2D neuromuscular co-cultures matured for 2 weeks and then treated with glutamate (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and Video 8).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures and video.

claim: A prior report of 2D human neuromuscular co-cultures performed functional assays only after 60 days of culture.
source: Indeed, a prior report of 2D human neuromuscular co-cultures performed functional assays only after 60 days of culture (Steinbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to prior work with citation.

claim: The average maximum functional connectivity length in 3D neuromuscular tissues was 1042.7 ± 104.5 μm at week 2 of co-culture.
source: Analysis of pre- and post-stimulation videos, to identify glutamate responsive fibers and substract spontaneously active fibers, indicated an average maximum functional connectivity length of 1042.7 ± 104.5 μm at this time-point.
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding from video analysis.

claim: The number of innervated fibers decreased as the distance from the MN cluster increased.
source: As expected, the number of innervated fibers decreased as the distance from the MN cluster increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Spontaneous endogenous endplate potentials (EPPs) were observed from single muscle fibers that were proximal to the MN cluster.
source: Using current clamp, we observed spontaneous endogenous endplate potentials (EPPs) from single muscle fibers that were proximal to the MN cluster (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), which were absent in muscle-alone cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Spontaneous endogenous EPPs were absent in muscle-alone cultures.
source: Using current clamp, we observed spontaneous endogenous endplate potentials (EPPs) from single muscle fibers that were proximal to the MN cluster (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C), which were absent in muscle-alone cultures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to muscle-alone cultures.

claim: Upon glutamate stimulation, the frequency of EPPs was increased.
source: Upon glutamate stimulation, the frequency of EPPs was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), whereas the amplitude remained unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Upon glutamate stimulation, the amplitude of EPPs remained unchanged.
source: Upon glutamate stimulation, the frequency of EPPs was increased (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), whereas the amplitude remained unchanged (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in EPP frequency upon glutamate stimulation supports the notion that the MNs were stimulated by glutamate to release neurotransmitter into the NMJ.
source: These results support the notion that the MNs were stimulated by glutamate to release neurotransmitter into the NMJ.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the EPP frequency data.

claim: An event resembling an action potential was captured in muscle fibers in response to glutamate stimulation.
source: Moreover, in these muscle fibers, we captured an event that resembled an action potential in response to glutamate stimulation (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Spontaneously occurring action potentials were never observed in neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: Notably, we never observed spontaneously occurring action potentials.
evidence: This is stated as an observation.

claim: 3D neuromuscular co-cultures support efficient functional innervation that occurs faster than previously reported for 2D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: Together, these studies indicate that 3D neuromuscular co-cultures support efficient functional innervation that occurs faster than previously reported for 2D neuromuscular co-cultures (Steinbeck et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion with citation to prior work.

claim: NRG1-β1 is expressed in PSC-derived MNs.
source: Using western blot experiments, we confirmed the expression of NRG1-β1 in our PSC-derived MNs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures.

claim: There was a significant increase in the expression of the CHRNE gene in co-cultures compared to muscle-alone cultures, in both 2D and 3D, after two weeks of culture.
source: We observed a significant increase in the expression of the CHRNE gene in co-cultures compared to muscle-alone cultures, in both 2D and 3D, after two weeks of culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting involvement of MN-derived trophic factors in CHRNE gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures.

claim: The increase in CHRNE expression in co-cultures suggests involvement of MN-derived trophic factors in CHRNE gene expression.
source: We observed a significant increase in the expression of the CHRNE gene in co-cultures compared to muscle-alone cultures, in both 2D and 3D, after two weeks of culture (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting involvement of MN-derived trophic factors in CHRNE gene expression.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the CHRNE expression data.

claim: Supplementing 2D and 3D muscle-alone cultures with recombinant NRG1-β1 (5 nM) resulted in a significant increase in CHRNE expression.
source: To test whether the increase can be associated with NRG1-β1-mediated induction of the CHRNE gene, we supplemented our 2D and 3D muscle-alone cultures with recombinant NRG1- β1 (5 nM) and detected a significant increase in CHRNE expression in the supplemented muscle fiber cultures (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures.

claim: Treating 3D muscle-alone cultures with motor neuron-derived conditioned media did not induce epsilon subunit gene expression above untreated 3D muscle alone cultures.
source: Treating 3D muscle-alone cultures with motor neuron-derived conditioned media did not induce epsilon subunit gene expression above untreated 3D muscle alone cultures (CHRNE 0.5 ± 0.4% of GAPDH expression), suggesting that MN axon contact with muscle fibers may be necessary to locally deliver concentrated neurotrophic factors and modulate epsilon gene expression in muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a finding with interpretation.

claim: MN axon contact with muscle fibers may be necessary to locally deliver concentrated neurotrophic factors and modulate epsilon gene expression in muscle fibers.
source: Treating 3D muscle-alone cultures with motor neuron-derived conditioned media did not induce epsilon subunit gene expression above untreated 3D muscle alone cultures (CHRNE 0.5 ± 0.4% of GAPDH expression), suggesting that MN axon contact with muscle fibers may be necessary to locally deliver concentrated neurotrophic factors and modulate epsilon gene expression in muscle fibers.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the conditioned media results.

claim: AChR epsilon protein expression was upregulated in 3D co-cultures, but not in 2D co-cultures.
source: We next evaluated AChR epsilon expression at the protein level and found that it was upregulated in 3D co-cultures, but not in 2D co-cultures (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4A-B.

claim: The upregulation of AChR epsilon protein expression in 3D co-cultures was accompanied by a significant increase in AChR beta.
source: The upregulation of AChR epsilon protein expression in 3D co-cultures was accompanied by a significant increase in AChR beta and no change in the AChR gamma subunit (Figure 4A–B), in support of studies concluding that gamma subunit transcription and translation does not appear to influence the onset or magnitude of epsilon expression (Witzemann et al., 1996; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and hinting that some embryonic AChRs may remain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4A-B.

claim: There was no change in the AChR gamma subunit in 3D co-cultures.
source: The upregulation of AChR epsilon protein expression in 3D co-cultures was accompanied by a significant increase in AChR beta and no change in the AChR gamma subunit (Figure 4A–B), in support of studies concluding that gamma subunit transcription and translation does not appear to influence the onset or magnitude of epsilon expression (Witzemann et al., 1996; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and hinting that some embryonic AChRs may remain.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4A-B.

claim: The AChR subunit data supports studies concluding that gamma subunit transcription and translation does not appear to influence the onset or magnitude of epsilon expression.
source: The upregulation of AChR epsilon protein expression in 3D co-cultures was accompanied by a significant increase in AChR beta and no change in the AChR gamma subunit (Figure 4A–B), in support of studies concluding that gamma subunit transcription and translation does not appear to influence the onset or magnitude of epsilon expression (Witzemann et al., 1996; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and hinting that some embryonic AChRs may remain.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations.

claim: The AChR subunit data hints that some embryonic AChRs may remain in 3D co-cultures.
source: The upregulation of AChR epsilon protein expression in 3D co-cultures was accompanied by a significant increase in AChR beta and no change in the AChR gamma subunit (Figure 4A–B), in support of studies concluding that gamma subunit transcription and translation does not appear to influence the onset or magnitude of epsilon expression (Witzemann et al., 1996; Yampolsky et al., 2008), and hinting that some embryonic AChRs may remain.
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on the data.

claim: MN-dependent changes in AChR subunit protein levels (beta, gamma, and epsilon) were not observed in 2D co-cultures.
source: MN-dependent changes in AChR subunit protein levels (beta, gamma, and epsilon) were not observed in 2D co-cultures (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4A.

claim: The observations support the notion that AChR epsilon protein stability is influenced by the degree of muscle fiber and NMJ activity.
source: These observations support the notion that AChR epsilon protein stability is influenced by the degree of muscle fiber and NMJ activity (Caroni et al., 1993; Missias et al., 1996; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations.

claim: WTX treatment resulted in a 46.47 ± 15% decrease in glutamate responsive tissue area in 3D neuromuscular tissues.
source: Consistently, we observed a 46.47 ± 15% (N = 3; p<0.05) decrease in glutamate responsive tissue area following glutamate stimulation in WTX pre-treated neuromuscular tissues (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding supported by Figure 4C.

claim: Analysis of calcium transients in individual fibers showed a 55.8 ± 1.8% decrease in response to glutamate stimulation after WTX treatment.
source: Similar results were obtained by analyzing calcium transients in individual fibers pre- and post WTX treatment in response to glutamate stimulation (Figure 4D; 55.8 ± 1.8% decrease).
evidence: This is stated as a quantitative finding supported by Figure 4D.

claim: A subset of WTX-treatment refractory single fibers was observed, indicating that not all AChRs in the 3D neuromuscular co-culture undergo the developmental switch by week 2.
source: This analysis also revealed a subset of WTX-treatment refractory single fibers (Figure 4C, white arrowheads), indicating that not all AChRs in the 3D neuromuscular co-culture undergo the developmental switch by this time point.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with interpretation.

claim: WTX treatment did not result in calcium transient changes in 2D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: We performed similar experiments on 2D neuromuscular co-cultures (Video 8), and 3D muscle-alone cultures (Video 10), but did not observe calcium transient changes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 8.

claim: WTX treatment did not result in calcium transient changes in 3D muscle-alone cultures.
source: We performed similar experiments on 2D neuromuscular co-cultures (Video 8), and 3D muscle-alone cultures (Video 10), but did not observe calcium transient changes.
evidence: This is stated as an observation supported by Video 10.

claim: 3D neuromuscular tissue GCaMP signal was not dampened by serial glutamate stimulation.
source: Importantly, 3D neuromuscular tissue GCaMP signal was not dampened by serial glutamate stimulation (see methods) excluding the possibility that GCaMP dampening was the result of glutamate neurotoxicity.
evidence: This is stated as a control experiment result.

claim: Localized deposition of complement on BTX stained AChRs was confirmed by staining for the complement C3c protein one-day after co-treating muscle tissues with MG IgG and active human complement.
source: Localized deposition of complement on BTX stained AChRs was confirmed by staining for the complement C3c protein one-day after co-treating muscle tissues with MG IgG and active human complement (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4E.

claim: There was a clear decrease in the area of stimuli responsive muscle fibers when tissues were treated with MG compared to healthy patient IgG.
source: Our analysis revealed a clear decrease in the area of stimuli responsive muscle fibers (Figure 4G and Videos 11–12) and a decline in the area of the tissue responsive to ACh stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D and Videos 11–12) when tissues were treated with MG compared to healthy patient IgG.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by Figure 4G and videos.

claim: There was a decline in the area of the tissue responsive to ACh stimulation when tissues were treated with MG compared to healthy patient IgG.
source: Our analysis revealed a clear decrease in the area of stimuli responsive muscle fibers (Figure 4G and Videos 11–12) and a decline in the area of the tissue responsive to ACh stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–D and Videos 11–12) when tissues were treated with MG compared to healthy patient IgG.
evidence: This is stated as a finding supported by supplementary figures and videos.

claim: Functional innervation is achieved in 3D, but not 2D neuromuscular co-cultures, within 2 weeks of culture.
source: We demonstrate that functional innervation is achieved in 3D, but not 2D neuromuscular co-cultures, within 2 weeks of culture.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding in the discussion.

claim: Innervation in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures is ~4 fold faster and more efficient than a prior report of a 2D human neuromuscular co-culture system.
source: Indeed, we find that innervation in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures is ~4 fold faster and more efficient than a prior report of a 2D human neuromuscular co-culture system (Steinbeck et al., 2016), and we show that this simplifies and expedites studies of myasthenia gravis in a dish.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to prior work with citation.

claim: CHRNE transcription is supported by MN co-culture in 2D and 3D.
source: With side-by-side comparisons of 2D and 3D muscle-alone and neuromuscular co-cultures, we confirmed that CHRNE transcription is supported by MN co-culture in 2D and 3D, and then show that the AChR epsilon subunit protein is only functionally integrated into the AChR in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparative studies.

claim: The AChR epsilon subunit protein is only functionally integrated into the AChR in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: With side-by-side comparisons of 2D and 3D muscle-alone and neuromuscular co-cultures, we confirmed that CHRNE transcription is supported by MN co-culture in 2D and 3D, and then show that the AChR epsilon subunit protein is only functionally integrated into the AChR in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding from comparative studies.

claim: This is the first report of a culture method to study the de novo AChR gamma to epsilon subunit developmental switch in culture.
source: Therefore, this is the first report of a culture method to study the de novo AChR gamma to epsilon subunit developmental switch in culture and to model diseases of the adult human NMJ in a dish.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty.

claim: This is the first report of a culture method to model diseases of the adult human NMJ in a dish.
source: Therefore, this is the first report of a culture method to study the de novo AChR gamma to epsilon subunit developmental switch in culture and to model diseases of the adult human NMJ in a dish.
evidence: This is stated as a claim of novelty.

claim: The 3D culture conditions lend to the maturation of multinucleated muscle fibers due to their capability to accommodate the inherent contractile nature of the muscle fibers in the long-term.
source: The value of 3D culture is reported in previous studies for other organs (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014), and in this study we provide the first quantitative evidence that 3D culture conditions lend to the maturation of multinucleated muscle fibers due to their capability to accommodate the inherent contractile nature of the muscle fibers in the long-term.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study with citation.

claim: 3D culture leads to muscle fiber hypertrophy, improved calcium handling, and muscle fiber maturation as evidenced by expression of adult forms of MHC, and elaborated clustering of AChRs.
source: This in turn leads to muscle fiber hypertrophy, improved calcium handling, and muscle fiber maturation as evidenced by expression of adult forms of MHC, and elaborated clustering of AChRs.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of 3D culture.

claim: 3D neuromuscular cultures are an ideal platform for studying NMJ synaptogenesis given the inherently long process required for functional NMJ development to occur.
source: This makes 3D neuromuscular cultures an ideal platform for studying NMJ synaptogenesis given the inherently long process required for functional NMJ development to occur.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion about the utility of the system.

claim: The properties of action potentials recorded in 3D neuromuscular co-cultures is consistent with the possibility that the cultures are not fully mature.
source: The properties of action potentials recorded in these cultures is consistent with the possibility that the 3D human neuromuscular co-cultures are not fully mature.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: Although the NMJs are functional and exhibit endogenous activity, most motor neurons are still in an immature state and do not trigger synchronous neurotransmitter release in response to glutamate application.
source: This suggests that although the NMJs are functional, exhibit endogenous activity, and that motor neurons respond to glutamate application by increasing the basal rate of neurotransmitter release, most motor neurons are still in an immature state and do not trigger synchronous neurotransmitter release in response to glutamate application.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the electrophysiology data.

claim: 3D neuromuscular cultures possess AChRs containing functional adult AChR epsilon subunit.
source: Perhaps most strikingly, 3D neuromuscular cultures possess AChRs containing functional adult AChR epsilon subunit, which is, to our knowledge, the first report of a system that supports the de novo gamma to epsilon AChR subunit switch in culture.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding.

claim: The success in achieving the AChR subunit switch may be due in part to the use of primary adult human myoblasts.
source: Given challenges associated with maturing hPSC-derived skeletal muscle fibers beyond embryonic-like states, we hypothesize that our success may be due in part to the use of primary adult human myoblasts.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis.

claim: CHRNE transcript expression is upregulated in both 2D and 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: Through an iterative comparison of 2D and 3D muscle alone and neuromuscular co-cultures, we found that CHRNE transcript expression is upregulated in both 2D and 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from comparative studies.

claim: Bathing 2D or 3D muscle fiber cultures with a high concentration of recombinant neuregulin-1 phenocopied the effect of MN co-culture on CHRNE transcript.
source: Bathing 2D or 3D muscle fiber cultures with a high concentration of recombinant neuregulin-1 phenocopied the effect of MN co-culture on CHRNE transcript, but CHRNE transcript levels were not induced in 3D muscle-alone culture treated with conditioned media from MNs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from treatment experiments.

claim: CHRNE transcript levels were not induced in 3D muscle-alone culture treated with conditioned media from MNs.
source: Bathing 2D or 3D muscle fiber cultures with a high concentration of recombinant neuregulin-1 phenocopied the effect of MN co-culture on CHRNE transcript, but CHRNE transcript levels were not induced in 3D muscle-alone culture treated with conditioned media from MNs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from treatment experiments.

claim: If CHRNE transcript induction is reliant on NRG-1, then localized MN-mediated delivery of the protein may be necessary to achieve physiologically relevant concentrations of the protein.
source: Since our PSC-derived motor neurons express neuregulin-1 protein, but we do not observe appreciable NMJ activity in our 2D neuromuscular co-cultures, we speculate that if CHRNE transcript induction is reliant on NRG-1, then localized MN-mediated delivery of the protein may be necessary to achieve physiologically relevant concentrations of the protein, and that transmission via the NMJ is not required.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the data.

claim: Transmission via the NMJ is not required for CHRNE transcript induction.
source: Since our PSC-derived motor neurons express neuregulin-1 protein, but we do not observe appreciable NMJ activity in our 2D neuromuscular co-cultures, we speculate that if CHRNE transcript induction is reliant on NRG-1, then localized MN-mediated delivery of the protein may be necessary to achieve physiologically relevant concentrations of the protein, and that transmission via the NMJ is not required.
evidence: This is stated as speculation based on the data.

claim: Epsilon protein levels further increased and its function was detected only in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
source: Importantly, epsilon protein levels further increased and its function was detected (WTX-responsivity) only in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-cultures.
evidence: This is stated as a key finding.

claim: The epsilon subunit of the AChR is subjected to post-transcriptional modifications and/or intracellular trafficking events that are only supported in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-culture.
source: Our culture data indicates that the epsilon subunit of the AChR is subjected to post-transcriptional modifications and/or intracellular trafficking events that are only supported in the context of 3D neuromuscular co-culture.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The observations that muscle fibers established in 3D culture are more mature and that 3D neuromuscular co-cultures exhibit spontaneous endogenous endplate potentials fit well with studies linking muscle fiber maturation state and activity to AChR subunit conversion and stability.
source: Indeed, our observations that muscle fibers established in 3D culture are more mature (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and 2) and that 3D neuromuscular co-cultures exhibit spontaneous endogenous endplate potentials (Figure 3 and Video 7) fit well with studies linking muscle fiber maturation state and activity to AChR subunit conversion and stability (Caroni et al., 1993; Missias et al., 1996; Witzemann et al., 2013; Xu and Salpeter, 1997; Yampolsky et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation with citations.
